intro: Ives begins his portrait of Emerson with overlapping fragments, not a tune neatly presented for development. Follow the contrast between crowded outbursts and quieter episodes; the rhythm of Beethoven’s Fifth helps connect them.
question: How can a recurring rhythm connect episodes that refuse a single continuous argument?

sections.label: Opening paragraphs
sections.mNote: overlapping fragments and repeated surges rather than one complete theme

sections.label: Quiet contrast
sections.mNote: a quieter span gathers force before another withdrawal

sections.label: Renewed argument
sections.mNote: fresh attacks emerge after a deep dip in level

sections.label: Central repetitions
sections.mNote: repeated melodic shapes accumulate weight, then recede

sections.label: Later episodes
sections.mNote: quiet lines grow into another extended crest

cues.title: Fragments before a theme
cues.text: The opening mixes short thematic fragments rather than presenting one complete tune. Listen for separate gestures interrupting and overlapping: material that sounds incidental here will matter again later in the sonata.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: sound builds from the opening into the 0:10–0:50 paragraph. Kyle Gann identifies seven overlapping themes on the first page, not seven separately timed entries: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Another push within the opening
cues.text: The opening renews its force after a brief easing. Follow the changing weight of the piano’s attacks rather than trying to reduce the whole paragraph to a single tune with accompaniment.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: boundary at 0:38; relative level rises from −18.0 dB at 0:30 to −11.0 dB at 0:45, with more detected attacks. Gann describes the overlapping opening: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: An impression, not a biography
cues.text: In the introduction to Essays Before a Sonata, Ives calls Emerson and Thoreau “composite pictures or impressions”. He explicitly rejects a programme of either man’s life or any one of his works.
cues.evidence: Charles Ives, Essays Before a Sonata, Introduction: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3673/pg3673-images.html#intro .

cues.title: Two ideas can coexist
cues.text: Throughout this movement, try following one hand without requiring the other to agree. Ives can place the two halves of the sonata’s recurring melody in different keys at once; dissonance need not erase the identity of either line.
cues.evidence: Gann identifies a passage combining the melody’s first half in C with its second half in A♭; this is a whole-movement listening strategy, not a claim that the passage begins here: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report places a local easing around 1:50–2:10.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Soloist and answering crowd
cues.text: Across the movement, compare the quieter, more individual lines with the weightier responses. The music grew from an unfinished Emerson concerto, in which Ives imagined the piano as Emerson and the orchestra as the responding multitude.
cues.evidence: Gann documents the 1910–11 concerto origin and Ives’s soloist/orchestra conception: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . This recording credits piano only; the orchestral comparison describes the conception, not additional performers. The report shows successive rises and dips through 2:15–3:35.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Unity without straight lines
cues.text: Ives defends Emerson’s habit of writing in phrases rather than a continuous logical sequence. In his essay, a large unity can emerge from scattered aspects of a subject; apparent confusion need not be the absence of a plan.
cues.evidence: Ives, Essays Before a Sonata, “Emerson”, section 2, beginning “A devotion to an end”: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3673/pg3673-images.html#emerson .

cues.title: A quieter space opens
cues.text: In this stretch the piano becomes quieter and the attacks spread out. Let the spaces separate the gestures: a soft passage is not merely an interval between the louder statements, but another way of making a line intelligible.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: strong boundary at 3:40; level falls from −11.0 dB at 3:30 to −29.9 dB at 3:45, with sparse attacks through 4:00. Gann describes a quiet verse episode among the early paragraphs: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: An organist’s formal training
cues.text: Ives studied composition with Horatio Parker at Yale and held the organist’s post at Center Church in New Haven. His later experiments came after sustained work in harmony, counterpoint, orchestration and form, not instead of that training.
cues.evidence: Jan Swafford, “Ives The Man: His Life”, “to the ivy”: https://charlesives.org/ives-man-his-life .

cues.title: A crest gives way
cues.text: The louder paragraph does not remain at its crest. Listen through the rapid loss of weight and the space it leaves before another attack starts the argument again.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: −9.9 dB and 4.0 detected attacks per second at 4:55 give way to −36.5 dB and 0.2 at 5:15. No exact cadence or rest is inferred. Episodic design: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: A fresh paragraph gathers force
cues.text: After the withdrawal, new attacks restore the piano’s weight. Hear the contrast between a fresh beginning and a literal restart: the movement repeatedly resumes its argument without returning to the same opening sentence.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: boundaries at 5:26 and 5:38; renewed activity reaches −12.0 dB at 5:40 and −12.3 dB at 5:50 after the 5:15 trough. Gann describes successive linked episodes: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: Printed at his own expense
cues.text: Ives paid for the sonata’s printing in 1920 and sent out two hundred copies in January 1921. Its accompanying essays were published separately; the unfamiliar score reached musicians together with an unusually extensive account of what its composer valued.
cues.evidence: Gann’s chronology distinguishes 1920 printing from January 1921 circulation: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . Ives’s Introduction says score and essays were separated to avoid a cumbersome volume: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3673/pg3673-images.html#intro .

cues.title: Repetition changes the weight
cues.text: In the broad central episode, a descending upper melody gains notes and weight through repetition while lower figures rise beneath it. Compare each statement with the preceding one: accumulation, rather than a new tune at every turn, shapes this paragraph.
cues.evidence: Gann describes the central episode’s descending melody, rising lower patterns and progressive enlargement: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report’s sustained central span around 6:10–7:50 grows towards strong 7:00–7:10 windows; placement is approximate, not bar-aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A crest with an afterthought
cues.text: The central span does not simply stop at its first crest. A brief retreat is followed by another push, then a much deeper withdrawal; follow the entire rise and fall as one extended paragraph.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: −8.6 dB at 7:10 falls to −18.8 at 7:20, returns to −9.0 at 7:40, then falls to −29.8 at 7:55. Boundaries at 7:22 and 7:34 support the internal contrasts. Central episode account: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: Nature is a reading
cues.text: Kyle Gann calls the central episode “nature”, relating its rising lower figures to the harmonic series and Emerson’s essay Nature. That is an analyst’s interpretation, not a scene-name supplied by Ives or a literal description of a landscape.
cues.evidence: Gann explicitly introduces “nature” as his own name and explains the association: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The cue reports his interpretation rather than upgrading it to Ives’s stated programme.

cues.title: From a line to many
cues.text: Through the later episodes, listen for the difference between a song-like line and several lines competing for attention. Gann traces a delicate Emerson-theme episode into fugue-like writing: a familiar idea can change its role without becoming a different theme.
cues.evidence: Gann describes that sequence after the central episode: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report anchors a broad rebuilding from the quiet 8:00–8:20 span towards 8:55–9:25, but does not separate voices or identify a fugue entry at this timestamp.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A text that kept changing
cues.text: The sonata did not remain fixed after its first printing. Ives began revising it by 1921, especially Emerson; a substantially revised edition appeared in 1947. The source for this performance does not identify which edition Liang used.
cues.evidence: Revision chronology: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . Recording source gives no edition: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ives_-_Piano_Sonata_No.2_-_I._Emerson_(Eric_Xi_Xin_Liang).flac .

cues.title: An extended late crest
cues.text: In this passage the piano gathers force and sustains it across several gestures. Notice that the larger shape is a plateau of activity, not just one emphatic chord followed by an immediate retreat.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: level rises after 10:05 and remains between −8.4 and −10.7 dB from 10:15 through 10:45; 10:20 is the loudest five-second window. No specific chord is identified. Episodic context: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: The argument loses weight
cues.text: After the sustained crest, the attacks thin and the piano recedes. Keep the preceding shapes in mind across the quieter gaps; the interruption prepares another accumulation rather than the end of the movement.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: level drops from −10.7 dB at 10:45 to −28.3 at 10:55 and −43.4 at 11:15; boundaries at 10:58 and 11:12. Gann’s later-return account supplies the broad context: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: Kirkpatrick brings the complete sonata
cues.text: John Kirkpatrick played the complete sonata privately at Cos Cob in November 1938, then gave its public premiere at New York’s Town Hall on 20 January 1939. Individual movements had already circulated in performances for nearly two decades.
cues.evidence: Gann’s timeline separates the private performance on 28 November 1938, the public premiere and earlier individual-movement performances: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: Continuity without literal repetition
cues.text: The late portion recalls material from earlier episodes, but not as a complete replay of the opening. Listen for familiar contours inside the renewed activity; recognition can concern a few notes before it concerns a whole section.
cues.evidence: Gann describes a recapitulation beginning with the first episode, not the introductory first page: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report shows renewed sustained activity from 11:25 onward; it does not establish a precise thematic-return boundary.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Beethoven as a connective rhythm
cues.text: The repeated-note gesture of Beethoven’s Fifth belongs to the movement’s larger network of themes. In the later forceful passages, listen for its short-short-short-long shape within the crowded chords rather than expecting a quotation to stand apart from Ives’s music.
cues.evidence: Gann identifies two large Beethoven-based climaxes and the motive’s pervasive role: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report places a late crest at 12:50–13:05, but does not independently identify the motive at 12:40; this is a listening invitation across that passage.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Beginning the long withdrawal
cues.text: The late crest yields to a less crowded, quieter passage. The movement still has time to unfold: a reduction in weight here begins a long dissolution rather than delivering a short closing cadence.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: level falls from −8.6 dB at 12:50 to −17.4 at 13:20 and −23.5 at 13:25; lower activity continues afterwards. Gann describes the extended dying-away close: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

cues.title: More than fate knocking
cues.text: At the end of his Emerson essay, Ives refuses to reduce Beethoven’s four-note gesture to fate knocking at a door. He instead imagines humanity addressing divine mysteries: the familiar rhythm carries a different philosophical claim inside this sonata.
cues.evidence: Ives, Essays Before a Sonata, final paragraph of “Emerson”, beginning “The Godliness of spiritual courage”: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3673/pg3673-images.html#emerson .

cues.title: Fragments survive the collapse
cues.text: Across the close, the Emerson theme is taken apart and the Beethoven rhythm remains in separated echoes. Follow those remnants through the gaps rather than expecting the crowded opening to return intact one final time.
cues.evidence: Gann describes the dismantled Emerson theme and Beethoven echoes in the close: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . The report supports a sparse closing span, including near-breaks at 14:05–14:15 and 14:50; exact notes and any optional viola are not identified.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sound after the attacks
cues.text: The last resonance continues after the attacks have ceased. Stay with the decay: the movement ends by letting its remaining sound disappear, not by adding a fresh emphatic answer.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: no detected attacks from 15:10 onward; relative level declines to −65.0 dB by 15:35 within the 937.8-second file. Gann describes the slow bass-motive ending: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

transitions.title: Weight gives way to space
transitions.how: The succession of forceful piano paragraphs yields to a quieter stretch with fewer attacks and more space between gestures. Ives does not require a conventional cadence to make that change legible: the contrast of density lets a line emerge from the preceding collisions. This map groups the early episodes together; it does not identify every thematic handover as a new section.
transitions.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: strong boundary at 3:40, level −11.0 dB at 3:30 to −29.9 at 3:45, attacks 3.2 to 0.8 per second. Gann describes the early chain of episodes, including a quiet verse theme: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

transitions.title: A withdrawal permits another beginning
transitions.how: The quieter paragraph has already grown into a crest before its sound falls away. Fresh piano attacks then rebuild the argument, rather than a sustained bass carrying the previous intensity across the join. The link is a change of pressure and spacing: a listener can hear a new paragraph without assigning the boundary to a particular key or to a literal return of the first page.
transitions.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: deep 5:15 trough between the 4:55–5:00 crest and renewed 5:20–5:40 attacks; boundaries at 5:26 and 5:38. Broad episodic design: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

transitions.title: Successive statements replace the collision
transitions.how: The central episode replaces the succession of argumentative fragments with a descending upper melody repeated and enlarged over rising lower patterns. Its continuity comes from those repeated shapes, not from removing all dissonance. As the texture gains weight, repetition makes the accumulation audible; the same paragraph will also be allowed to recede rather than ending only in an outburst.
transitions.evidence: Gann’s central-episode account supplies the melodic directions and enlargement: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: the more sparsely attacked 6:05–6:40 span leads into the broad 6:45–7:45 crest and 7:55 withdrawal. The 6:10 map point is approximate, not an aligned first note.

transitions.title: The central span releases its hold
transitions.how: The repeated central paragraph releases its accumulated weight. A quieter line opens another chain of episodes, later growing into more crowded counterpoint. The decisive change is from a sustained accumulation to a new, lightly articulated beginning; a soft entrance here is a structural hinge, not simply the same climax played at a lower dynamic.
transitions.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: strong boundary at 8:02, with level falling from −9.0 dB at 7:40 to −30.6 at 8:00; the 7:55 window has no detected attacks. Gann describes the song-like episode after the central span and its later fugue-like continuation: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

transitions.title: A near-break precedes renewed activity
transitions.how: The extended late crest subsides almost to a break before a new accumulation begins. The contrast depends on the piano’s attacks: they become sparse, then regain weight and frequency. Earlier material will reappear in this late region, but the map marks the audible hinge rather than pretending to locate the exact first note of a recapitulation.
transitions.evidence: cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: strongest boundary at 11:12; −43.4 dB at 11:15 rises to −14.3 by 11:25, with renewed attacks. Gann documents a late recapitulation but supplies no Liang-specific alignment: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

transitions.title: The crowded argument breaks into remnants
transitions.how: After the later climax, Ives dismantles rather than recapitulates the entire argument. The Emerson theme breaks into remnants and the Beethoven rhythm persists in separated echoes; spacing and reduced weight make fragments that once collided sound isolated. The long close retains tonal tensions instead of providing a single triumphant chord as an answer.
transitions.evidence: Gann describes the post-climax dissolution, including Beethoven echoes in distant keys: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 . cache/analysis/ives-concord-emerson.txt: sustained fall after 13:15, −23.5 dB by 13:25, followed by sparse 14-minute and final-decay windows. No timestamped key change or viola entrance is asserted.

composer.background:
Charles Ives grew up in Danbury, Connecticut, where his father George directed bands, played the cornet and taught music. George had served as a Union bandmaster during the American Civil War. The son’s later recollections describe experiments with bands playing different tunes, quarter-tone instruments and singing in one key against an accompaniment in another. These accounts are filtered through a son’s memory of his father, but the musical questions they pose recur in the scores: how far apart can independent parts move before they stop making a perceptible whole?

Ives was also trained in conventional musicianship. He became a paid church organist as a teenager and wrote the organ Variations on America in 1891. At Yale, from 1894 to 1898, Horatio Parker taught him counterpoint, orchestration and large-scale form. His First Symphony belongs to that apprenticeship, with audible debts to European symphonic writing. George died in 1894, shortly after Charles entered Yale. The practical musical culture of Danbury subsequently became both a source of material and a standard against which Ives judged the professional concert world.
composer.epithet: A church organist and insurance executive who made hymns, marching bands and incompatible tempos coexist inside concert music.
